lesson.title: Two Different Questions: Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance
lesson.summary: Statistical significance and practical significance are two separate questions, whether an effect is real and whether it is big enough to matter, and a complete conclusion has to answer both.
lesson.body:
Pulling the last two chapters together: statistical significance asks whether an effect is likely to be real rather than a fluke of sampling; practical significance asks whether that effect, assuming it's real, is large enough to matter. A result can land on either side of each question independently, which gives four possible combinations. Statistically and practically significant: the hours-studied and quiz-score example running through this unit, where a large, real effect (1.8 points per hour, R² = 98.6%) also cleared the statistical bar (p < 0.0001) even with a tiny sample of just six students. Statistically significant but not practically significant: the hypothetical height and heart-rate example from the last chapter, a real but tiny effect (0.6 bpm across a foot of height) that only cleared the statistical bar because the sample size was enormous (n = 500,000). Not statistically significant but potentially practically significant if real: a genuinely large effect that a small, noisy sample simply failed to detect with enough confidence, a result worth pursuing with more data rather than dismissing outright. Neither statistically nor practically significant: no meaningful effect, and the data show it plainly.

The mechanism behind all of this is worth holding onto, since it's what makes the distinction more than just semantic. A p-value is the product of three things tangled together: the size of the effect (b1), the amount of leftover noise (captured by s), and the sample size (which drives SSxx, and therefore SE(b1)). Because sample size is one of the ingredients, the exact same true effect can produce an unremarkable p-value in a small study and an overwhelming one in a massive study, without the underlying real-world relationship changing size at all. Effect size, R² or the slope itself in its original units, is the one piece of that picture that doesn't move just because n changes, which is exactly why it, and not the p-value alone, is the right tool for judging whether a result matters.

A practical two-step habit for reading any regression result, on this course's exams and afterward: first, ask the statistical question, is there good evidence the slope isn't exactly zero (a small p-value, or a confidence interval that excludes zero)? Then, separately, ask the practical question, in the real, original units of the problem, is the estimated slope, and its confidence interval, large enough that it would actually change a decision, a diagnosis, a policy, or a purchase? Both questions require looking at the actual numeric value and its units, not just whether some threshold like p < 0.05 was crossed.

This closes the loop on the whole unit. The chapters on the t-test for the slope, its standard error, the LINE conditions, and writing a proper conclusion were all about answering the statistical significance question carefully and honestly. Effect size and practical significance exist because rigor about 'is this real' is necessary but not sufficient. A complete statistical argument, the kind expected on the AP exam and in any serious use of data, answers both 'is it real' and 'does it matter,' and treats them as the two separate questions they actually are.
